title: Abrupt dry cough and fever in a 34-year-old builder
desc: This station is a focused acute cough history and respiratory examination of Charlie, a 34-year-old builder seen in general practice. He has had an abrupt dry cough with coughing fits for 3 days, with fever, malaise, a sore throat and nasal congestion. A friend has also been coughing, and he did not have the flu vaccine this year. In Part 2 the candidate interprets his observations and a respiratory PCR swab, diagnoses uncomplicated influenza A and answers his COVID question. They then give supportive care without antibiotics or antivirals, advise him on infection control, vaccination and quitting smoking, and safety-net.
focus: Acute cough: a focused respiratory history and review of systems, then recognising and managing uncomplicated influenza in general practice
stem: You are a medical student on placement in a general practice. It is July. Charlie is a 34-year-old builder who has come to see you because of a cough. Your supervising GP is available in the next room.
tasks: Take a focused history from Charlie, including a respiratory system review, and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you Charlie's observations and the result of his respiratory PCR swab. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and your safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Charlie, a 34-year-old builder. You feel rotten: tired, hot and achy. You cough in short, dry bursts now and then during the consultation, and your throat hurts when you do. You are friendly and chatty, and a bit worried you have COVID. When the candidate says what they would examine, the examiner gives the findings from the Exam findings below.

Opening line: "I've had this bad cough for a few days now. It's been bothering me a lot."

The cough (give only when asked):

  • Onset: it came on suddenly 3 days ago. You were fine the day before.
  • Character: dry. You aren't bringing anything up, and there has been no blood.
  • Pattern: you get coughing fits several times a day.
  • Better: cough lollies help a bit.
  • Before: you had a similar episode about 2 years ago, and it went away on its own.
  • Impact: you took yesterday off work because you felt too unwell to be on site. Your throat really hurts from all the coughing.
  • Only if asked: no whooping noise when you breathe in after a fit, and no vomiting after coughing.

Contacts (give when asked about sick contacts, or raise it when you ask your questions): "One of my friends has been coughing a lot as well. Could I have caught it off him?" You saw him a few days before your cough started.

Respiratory system review (only if asked about each):

  • Yes: very mild shortness of breath, but only straight after a coughing fit, and fine otherwise. Sore throat. Blocked, stuffy nose. Fevers: you have felt hot and sweaty, but you haven't measured it. You feel generally unwell, achy all over and run down. You are very tired.
  • No: no wheeze. No runny nose and no sneezing, which is different from your usual hay fever. No sharp chest pain when you breathe in. No weight loss. Your appetite is not really affected.
  • If asked about headache: a mild headache with the fevers.
  • If asked: you are drinking plenty of fluids and passing urine normally. No confusion, rash or stiff neck.

Past medical history: you have been well in general. You get hay fever (allergic rhinitis). You had your appendix out at 14 and an Achilles tendon repair at 18. You have had 2 COVID vaccines. You did not get the flu vaccine this year. No asthma, no lung problems, no diabetes or heart problems.

Medications: an antihistamine tablet from the chemist for hay fever. You can't remember the name. Nothing else, apart from the cough lollies.

Allergies: pollen and dust mites. No allergies to medicines.

Family history: your dad has high blood pressure and your mum has COPD ("emphysema, from smoking").

Social history:

  • You smoke about half a pack a day (about 10 cigarettes) and have done since you were 20.
  • You drink about 6 beers a week, on weekends.
  • You are a builder.
  • You live in a flat with housemates. They are well. No one at home is pregnant, elderly or has a small baby.
  • No recent overseas travel.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you think it is "a bug going around". You are worried it might be COVID, because you don't want to give it to your housemates or the crew at work. You would like to know what it is, get something for your throat, and know when you can go back to work.

Questions to raise (if not already covered, near the end of Part 1):

  • "Is it possible that I have COVID?"
  • "One of my friends has been coughing a lot as well. Could I have caught it off him?"

Exam findings (the examiner gives these only when the candidate says what they would examine):

  • General: tired, flushed young man, sitting comfortably and speaking in full sentences. Short bursts of dry cough. Not distressed, not cyanosed. Weight 82 kg if asked.
  • Vital signs (10:10): HR 98 beats/min regular; BP 126/78 mmHg; RR 18/min; SpO2 97% on room air; temperature 38.3 °C.
  • Hands: mild nicotine staining of the right index and middle fingers. No clubbing. Warm peripheries.
  • Hydration: mucous membranes moist. Capillary refill under 2 seconds.
  • Ears, nose and throat: pharynx red. Tonsils not enlarged, with no exudate. Nasal mucosa swollen and congested with no discharge. Ear canals and eardrums normal. No cervical lymphadenopathy. Neck supple.
  • Chest: trachea midline. Expansion symmetrical. Percussion resonant throughout. Vesicular breath sounds throughout. No crackles, wheeze or bronchial breathing. No pleural rub.
  • Cardiovascular: heart sounds dual with no murmur. No peripheral oedema.
  • Skin: no rash.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self as a medical student, confirms the patient's identity, explains the purpose of the consultation and gains consent.
Opens with an open question, then focuses. Uses plain language and acknowledges how unwell he feels and his sore throat.
History
Characterises the cough:

kids.x: Onset and duration: abrupt onset 3 days ago.
Asks about sputum and haemoptysis: dry, with no sputum and no blood.
Pattern and modifiers: coughing fits several times a day, eased a little by cough lollies, and a similar episode 2 years ago.
Impact: took yesterday off work, and his throat really hurts from coughing.

check.x: Asks about sick contacts and finds a friend who has also been coughing a lot.
check.d: Credit if the candidate asks, or if they explore it properly when Charlie raises it.

check.x: Respiratory system review: elicits the positives:

kids.x: Very mild breathlessness, only after coughing fits.

check.x: Respiratory system review: asks about the negatives that point to other diagnoses:
check.d: Source marking: the review of systems earns marks for the positives and negatives together.

kids.x: Pneumonia or more serious illness: no pleuritic chest pain and no breathlessness at rest.
Asthma or allergic rhinitis: no wheeze, runny nose or sneezing.
Chronic or sinister causes: no weight loss or anorexia.

check.x: Takes a past medical history:

kids.x: Surgery: appendicectomy at 14 and Achilles tendon repair at 18.
Asks about vaccination: COVID vaccinated twice, and no influenza vaccine this year.

check.x: Takes a medication and allergy history: antihistamine for allergic rhinitis; allergic to pollen and dust mites, with no drug allergies.
Takes a family history: father with hypertension and mother with COPD.
Takes a social history:

kids.x: Smoking: half a pack a day since age 20 (about 7 pack-years).
Alcohol: about 6 beers a week on weekends.
Occupation and living situation: builder, lives in a flat with housemates (contacts who could catch it).

check.x: Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations, including his worry about COVID and about passing it on, and his question about catching it from his friend.
Examination

Inspects him generally and requests a full set of vital signs including temperature and SpO2. Identifies fever (38.3 °C) with a high-normal heart rate (98) and normal RR, SpO2 (97% on room air) and BP.
Examines the ears, nose and throat and the cervical lymph nodes: red pharynx without tonsillar exudate, congested nose, normal ears, no lymphadenopathy.
Examines the chest: tracheal position, expansion, percussion and auscultation. Finds a clear chest with no crackles, bronchial breathing or wheeze.
Assesses hydration (mucous membranes, capillary refill), listens to the heart and checks for a rash or neck stiffness.
Interpretation

Observations: febrile with a high-normal heart rate, settling slightly by the afternoon (38.0 °C, HR 94). RR, SpO2 and BP normal throughout. States he is not hypoxic or septic and can be managed at home.
Respiratory PCR: influenza A detected.
Respiratory PCR: SARS-CoV-2, influenza B, RSV and Bordetella pertussis not detected. Uses this to answer the COVID question.
States the most likely diagnosis is uncomplicated influenza A, justified by: abrupt onset, dry cough, fever, malaise, sore throat, a coughing contact and no influenza vaccine this year.
check.d: Source marking: influenza with reasoning. Credit the diagnosis with at least four of the listed supporting features.

check.x: Gives the feature against at least three differentials: COVID-19 (PCR negative), pertussis (PCR negative, cough of only 3 days, no whoop), pneumonia (clear chest, SpO2 97%, no pleuritic pain), asthma exacerbation (no wheeze).
Management
Manages him at home with supportive care, stating that a chest X-ray and bloods are not needed when the chest is clear and saturation is normal.
Symptomatic care: rest, oral fluids, paracetamol or ibuprofen for fever, aches and sore throat (at standard doses), and lozenges or honey for the cough and throat.
check.d: Accept paracetamol 1 g orally every 4 to 6 hours (maximum 4 g in 24 hours) or ibuprofen 200 to 400 mg orally every 6 to 8 hours with food (maximum 1200 mg daily, non-prescription).

check.x: States that antibiotics are not indicated, because this is a viral infection with no evidence of bacterial pneumonia.

States that an antiviral (oseltamivir) is not routinely needed, because it is more than 48 hours since onset and he is not at higher risk of complications. Antivirals are reserved for severe illness or higher-risk patients.
check.d: Accept a statement that antivirals are not needed in an otherwise healthy adult beyond 48 hours. Do not penalise a candidate who says they would discuss it with the supervising GP.

check.x: Gives infection control advice: stay home from work while unwell (with a medical certificate), cover coughs, wash hands, and keep away from vulnerable people, including housemates where possible.
Covers prevention:

kids.x: Recommends an annual influenza vaccine, starting once he has recovered.
Gives brief smoking cessation advice and offers support (Quitline 13 7848, pharmacotherapy, follow-up).

check.x: Explains in plain words that this is the flu, not COVID, that he probably caught it from his friend, and checks his understanding.
Safety netting

Gives specific red flags in plain words, each with its action: breathless at rest or struggling to breathe, chest pain, blue lips or confusion (call 000); coughing up blood, unable to keep fluids down, or getting worse after starting to improve (GP or ED the same day).
check.d: Credit at least three red flags, each with the correct action.

check.x: Explains the expected course: the fever usually settles within a few days, but the cough and tiredness can last 1 to 2 weeks or more.
Arranges follow-up: GP review if he is not improving within a few days, or if the cough persists beyond about 3 weeks; a booked visit for the flu vaccine and quit support.

part2.lead: The practice nurse took Charlie's observations, and a nasopharyngeal and throat swab was couriered to the laboratory for a respiratory PCR. Charlie has come back late this afternoon for the result. Here are his observations and his swab result.
part2.patient:
When the candidate explains, Charlie asks, if not already covered:

  • "So it's definitely not COVID?"
  • "Did I catch it off my mate?"
  • "Don't I need antibiotics, or that flu tablet?"
  • "When can I go back to work? I need a certificate for yesterday and today."

He is relieved it is not COVID. He is a little reluctant about quitting smoking, but agrees to think about it if it is raised without lecturing.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Taken by the practice nurse, seated, on room air. 10:10 on arrival; 16:05 when he returned for the swab result. No medicines given in the practice.
handover.model:
Read: at 10:10, temperature 38.3 °C and HR 98, with RR 18, SpO2 97% on room air, BP 126/78 and alert. At 16:05, temperature 38.0 °C and HR 94, with the other values unchanged.

For Charlie: fever with a high-normal heart rate in keeping with a viral illness. Normal RR, saturation and BP mean no hypoxia, no sepsis and no sign of pneumonia.

What it changes: no adult observation chart applies in general practice. Nothing here calls for hospital transfer, a chest X-ray or bloods. He can be managed at home with safety netting.

rows.note: On arrival, seated at rest; coughing intermittently
Returned for swab result, seated at rest

handover.label: Respiratory PCR swab
handover.result: Nasopharyngeal and throat swab, collected 10:30 today. Multiplex respiratory nucleic acid test (PCR). Laboratory comment: influenza A RNA detected. Laboratory-confirmed influenza is notifiable and has been notified to the public health unit by the laboratory.
handover.model:
Read: influenza A detected. Influenza B, SARS-CoV-2, RSV and Bordetella pertussis not detected.

For Charlie: this confirms the clinical picture of influenza A: abrupt onset, dry cough, fever, malaise, sore throat, a coughing contact and no vaccine this year. It answers his question: this is not COVID-19. Pertussis, which his coughing fits might have suggested, is not detected.

What it changes: supportive care with no antibiotics. He is beyond 48 hours from onset and not at higher risk, so an antiviral is not routinely indicated. Advise him to stay home and on hygiene measures. The laboratory has notified the result, so the GP does not need to.

ask: You are now presenting Charlie to your supervising GP. Please give an ISBAR handover of Charlie, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Charlie now, here in general practice.
Before Charlie goes home, what would you tell him and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: self, medical student. Charlie, 34-year-old builder.
  • Situation: 3 days of abrupt dry cough with fever. Influenza A on PCR.
  • Background: coughing fits, sore throat, congestion, malaise, fatigue. Breathless only after coughing fits. Friend coughing. No flu vaccine this year; COVID vaccinated twice. Allergic rhinitis on an antihistamine. Smoker, about 7 pack-years. Lives with housemates.
  • Assessment: T 38.3 then 38.0 °C, with a high-normal HR of 98 then 94. RR 18, SpO2 97% on room air, BP normal. Chest clear. PCR: influenza A detected; SARS-CoV-2, influenza B, RSV and pertussis not detected. Uncomplicated influenza A, with no pneumonia or hypoxia.
  • Recommendation: home with supportive care. No antibiotics. No antiviral (beyond 48 hours, not high risk). Off work with a certificate. Flu vaccine and quit support. Safety-net. Could you review him with me?

Most likely: uncomplicated influenza A. For it: abrupt onset, dry cough, fever, malaise and fatigue, sore throat, nasal congestion, a coughing contact, no vaccine this year, and influenza A on PCR.

  • COVID-19: similar features, and it is his worry. Against: SARS-CoV-2 not detected.
  • Pertussis: coughing fits. Against: only 3 days, no whoop or vomiting after coughing, PCR negative.
  • Community-acquired pneumonia (including secondary bacterial): fever, mild breathlessness, smoker. Against: dry cough, no pleuritic pain, clear chest, SpO2 97%, RR 18.
  • Viral-triggered asthma or allergic airway flare: atopy, similar episode before. Against: no wheeze, a clear chest, no runny nose or sneezing.
  • Other viral infection or acute bronchitis: possible. Against: influenza A confirmed, RSV not detected.

1. Disposition: uncomplicated, with normal saturation and a clear chest, so home. No chest X-ray or bloods needed.
  2. Supportive care: rest, oral fluids, paracetamol or ibuprofen at standard doses, lozenges or honey. Continue the antihistamine.
  3. No antibiotics: viral, with no sign of bacterial pneumonia.
  4. Antivirals: not routinely indicated. He is more than 48 hours from onset and not in a higher-risk group. Oseltamivir is for severe illness or higher-risk patients.
  5. Infection control: stay home while unwell, with a medical certificate. Cough etiquette and hand hygiene. Avoid vulnerable people.
  6. Public health: notified by the laboratory.
  7. Prevention: annual flu vaccine once recovered. Brief smoking cessation advice (Quitline 13 7848, NRT or other pharmacotherapy).
  8. Discuss with the supervising GP.

• In plain words: this is the flu, not COVID. He most likely caught it from his friend through coughing and sneezing; it usually shows 1 to 4 days after contact. Antibiotics do not work on viruses.
  • Expected course: the fever usually settles in a few days. The cough and tiredness may last 1 to 2 weeks or more.
  • Red flags:
    • call 000 if breathless at rest or struggling to breathe, chest pain, blue lips, or confusion or drowsiness
    • GP or ED the same day if coughing up blood, unable to keep fluids down, or getting better then worse again with new fever or coloured phlegm
  • Work and home: stay off work until he feels well. Cover coughs and wash hands.
  • Follow-up: GP review if not improving in a few days, or if the cough lasts beyond about 3 weeks. Book the flu vaccine and a quit-smoking follow-up.

guide:
In Part 1 the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. Charlie raises his COVID and "caught it off my friend" questions near the end if the candidate has not drawn them out. A good answer in Part 1 is that COVID-19 and influenza cannot be told apart clinically and that a respiratory PCR swab would answer this. In Part 2, hand over both results together and ask the four questions in order. Charlie puts his questions while the candidate explains. Credit the interpretation items whether they come up in the ISBAR or in the diagnosis answer.

The source was an 8-minute history with a respiratory system review and a differential. The examination findings, observations and PCR result have been written to fit it. Myalgia and headache are not in the source script, but they are in its teaching notes, so they are given only if asked. The source credits the sick contact and the missed flu vaccine as reasoning for influenza. Both are marked in the history and in the diagnosis item.

A high-performing candidate characterises the cough and works through a systematic respiratory review that picks up the fever, malaise, sore throat and congestion and the relevant negatives. They ask about contacts and vaccination, take a complete background history including smoking in pack-years, and examine the throat and chest with full vital signs. In Part 2 they call this uncomplicated influenza A, use the PCR to answer the COVID question, and justify the differentials. They give supportive care without antibiotics, explain why an antiviral is not needed, give clear infection control, vaccination and quit-smoking advice, and safety-net with specific red flags.

A borderline candidate takes a scattered history and misses the contact or the vaccination history. They prescribe antibiotics, or oseltamivir without reasoning, order a chest X-ray despite a clear chest, or end with "come back if you're worried".
explain:
Diagnosis: uncomplicated influenza A

Charlie is a previously well 34-year-old. Three days ago a dry cough began abruptly, with coughing fits, fever, malaise, fatigue, a sore throat and nasal congestion. A friend has been coughing, and he did not have this year's influenza vaccine. That is a classic influenza-like illness, and the PCR confirms influenza A. His chest is clear and his saturation is normal, so this is uncomplicated influenza that can be managed at home.

About influenza

  • The virus: influenza A, B and C. Influenza A is the most common, and A and B cause the seasonal winter epidemics.
  • Spread: by respiratory droplets and contaminated surfaces, so always ask about sick contacts.
  • Incubation: 1 to 4 days, average 2. This fits catching it from his friend.
  • Severity: about 75% of infections are asymptomatic or mild.
  • Features: abrupt onset of non-productive cough, fever, myalgia, headache, malaise, sore throat and nasal congestion.
  • Prevention: an annual vaccine is available.

Taking the history: the respiratory system review

Characterise the cough: onset, duration, sputum and haemoptysis, pattern, triggers and relieving factors, previous episodes and impact. Then work through the respiratory review:

  • Breathlessness: at rest or on exertion.
  • Wheeze.
  • Chest pain: particularly pleuritic.
  • Upper airway symptoms: sore throat, congestion, runny nose, sneezing.
  • Systemic features: fever, malaise, fatigue, weight loss, anorexia.

The negatives matter as much as the positives. No pleuritic pain or breathlessness at rest argues against pneumonia. No wheeze argues against asthma. No runny nose or sneezing makes this unlike his usual allergic rhinitis. No weight loss or anorexia, together with an acute course, argues against a chronic cause. Contacts, vaccination status, smoking and the living situation shape both the diagnosis and the advice.

Differentials

  • COVID-19: clinically indistinguishable from influenza, so test. Here SARS-CoV-2 is not detected.
  • Pertussis: paroxysmal coughing fits should prompt the question. It typically has a longer course, with an inspiratory whoop or vomiting after coughing, and matters because of infants at home. It is not detected here.
  • Community-acquired pneumonia, including secondary bacterial pneumonia after influenza: suspect it with productive cough, pleuritic pain, focal chest signs, tachypnoea or hypoxia, or a second worsening after initial improvement.
  • Viral-triggered asthma: consider it in an atopic patient. There is no wheeze here.

Interpreting the results

Observations: fever with a high-normal heart rate (98, then 94), in keeping with fever, and normal RR, SpO2 and BP. In adults tachycardia means a heart rate above 100/min, so his heart rate is within normal limits. He is not hypoxic or septic and needs no imaging or bloods.

PCR: influenza A detected. SARS-CoV-2, influenza B, RSV and pertussis are not detected. Laboratory-confirmed influenza is notifiable in Australia, and the laboratory notifies it.

Management (eTG)

  • Supportive care for an otherwise healthy adult: rest, fluids, and paracetamol or ibuprofen for fever, aches and sore throat: paracetamol 1 g orally every 4 to 6 hours, maximum 4 g in 24 hours; ibuprofen 200 to 400 mg orally every 6 to 8 hours with food, maximum 1200 mg daily (non-prescription). Lozenges or honey can soothe the cough.
  • Antibiotics: they do not treat influenza and are not indicated without evidence of secondary bacterial infection.
  • Antivirals:
    • Neuraminidase inhibitors such as oseltamivir 75 mg orally twice daily for 5 days are recommended for people with severe or complicated influenza, and for those at higher risk of complications.
    • Higher-risk groups include people aged 65 years or more, pregnant women, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, people with chronic heart, lung, renal, neurological or metabolic disease, immunocompromised people, and severe obesity.
    • In otherwise healthy adults the benefit is modest, mainly shortening symptoms by about a day, and only if started within 48 hours of onset.
    • Charlie is beyond 48 hours and not in a higher-risk group, so an antiviral is not routinely needed.
  • Infection control: stay home from work while unwell (provide a certificate), cover coughs and sneezes, wash hands, and avoid contact with vulnerable people.

Prevention

The Australian Immunisation Handbook recommends annual influenza vaccination for everyone aged 6 months and over. Infection with one strain does not protect against the others, so Charlie should be vaccinated once he has recovered and every year after. His smoking (about 7 pack-years) raises his risk of respiratory infections and their complications, and his mother has COPD. This consultation is a good chance for brief advice using the RACGP Ask, Advise, Help approach: Quitline 13 7848 and pharmacotherapy such as nicotine replacement or varenicline, with follow-up.

Safety netting

The fever usually settles within a few days, but the cough and fatigue can last 1 to 2 weeks or longer. Tell him clearly when to get help:

  • Call 000: breathlessness at rest, difficulty breathing, chest pain, blue lips, confusion or drowsiness.
  • See a GP or go to ED the same day: coughing up blood, being unable to keep fluids down, or improving and then worsening again with new fever or coloured sputum (possible secondary bacterial pneumonia).
  • GP review: if he is not improving within a few days, or if the cough persists beyond about 3 weeks.
points: Abrupt-onset dry cough with fever, malaise, sore throat and nasal congestion during flu season, especially with a sick contact and no vaccine this year, is influenza until proven otherwise.
A respiratory system review needs the negatives as well as the positives: no pleuritic pain, breathlessness at rest or focal chest signs argues against pneumonia, and no wheeze argues against asthma.
COVID-19 and influenza cannot be told apart clinically, so a respiratory PCR answers the patient's question and guides isolation advice.

Uncomplicated influenza in a healthy adult needs supportive care, not antibiotics. Oseltamivir is for severe illness or higher-risk patients, and its benefit in healthy adults is modest and limited to the first 48 hours.
Advise staying home while unwell, cough etiquette and hand hygiene. Recommend the annual flu vaccine for everyone aged 6 months and over, and use the visit for brief smoking cessation advice.
Safety-net with specific red flags: breathlessness at rest, chest pain or confusion means 000, and getting worse again after improving means same-day review.
